passages.context: The complete chapter heading and body were inspected at artifact lines 14194–14214. Augustine frames and rejects the proposal that allegedly good demons should be cultivated as mediators to blessedness, directing rational creatures instead to the true God. This is a theological argument against demonic cult and mediation, not an exorcistic rubric, case account, classification of symptoms, or operational instruction.
passages.notes: This exact tracked 1871 Dods English witness is not a critical Latin control. The bounded chapter does not by itself establish every aspect of Augustine's demonology or an author-wide negative result.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17603-17633, under the heading 'That the world and time had both one beginning, and the one did not anticipate the other'. Augustine argues that time cannot precede creation, reads 'in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth' as excluding anything made earlier, and closes on the order of the first six or seven days through the seventh day's rest. The heading occupies lines 17603-17604 and the body begins at 17606.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17636-17677, under the heading 'Of the nature of the first days, which are said to have had morning and evening, before there was a sun'. Augustine holds that the first three days passed without a sun, that light was made by the word of God and separated from the darkness, and that what kind of light it was lies beyond the senses. The remainder of the chapter, at lines 17648-17677, offers the figurative reading of morning and evening as the creature's knowledge and runs through the sixth day. The heading occupies lines 17636-17637.
passages.notes: The recorded text is the exact whitespace join of artifact lines 17639-17647, stopping mid-line at 'believe it.' The fourth day is named at line 17641 as the premise that the sun did not yet exist, not expounded, so Genesis 1:14-19 stands outside the recorded extent.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 20768-20812, under the heading 'Of that death which can affect an immortal soul, and of that to which the body is subject': the soul called immortal because it does not cease to live and feel, the body called mortal because it can be forsaken of all life; the death of the soul when God forsakes it and the death of the body when the soul forsakes it; the death of the whole man as the compound of the two; the second death that follows; the appeal to Matthew 10:28; and the closing judgment that the first and bodily death is 'to the good it is good, and evil to the evil' while the second can be good for none. The chapter is the tradition's most careful early statement of what the word death is being used to name.
passages.notes: The chapter heading occupies artifact lines 20768-20769 and the body begins at 20771. passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 21111-21195, under the heading 'Whether one can both be living and dead at the same time': the three times and three corresponding states; the argument that a man is never in death because before death he lives and after it he is dead; the comparison with the unlocatable present instant of time; the question whether it follows that there is no death of the body at all; Augustine's refusal to draw that conclusion; his decision to keep speaking in the customary way on the warrant of scriptural usage, quoting Psalm 6:6; and the closing remark about the damned as endlessly dying. The chapter is the classical statement of the aporia about the moment of death, and Augustine leaves it unresolved.
passages.notes: The chapter heading is at artifact line 21111 and the body begins at 21113. The recorded text is the exact whitespace join of complete artifact lines 21128-21133 and therefore opens and closes mid-sentence; the sentence a consumer usually wants begins 'And thus, before death' at the tail of line 21127 and ends at 'comprehended in the state of death.' inside line 21133. The related chapters are 13.9 (whether the moment of death belongs to the dying or the dead) and 13.10 (life as a race toward death), immediately preceding in the same artifact. Book XIII of this printing is Dods 1871 volume I.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 13015-13068. It says human dominion over humans was not part of the created natural order, traces slavery to sin, also treats servitude as penal within fallen order, instructs faithful service where civil freedom is unavailable, and looks toward the passing of all unrighteousness and human power.
passages.notes: Detached edition notes for the chapter are at artifact lines 13806-13814. The passage is retained as evidence for Augustine's own complex argument. It does not by itself establish an abolitionist program, justify enslavement, or settle the document's wider evaluation of his legacy.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17748-17782: Augustine's 'amicable controversy' with tender-hearted Christians who held that the damned would be delivered after a fixed term, his report that Origen went further and included the devil and his angels, his statement that the Church condemned Origen for this and for the ceaseless alternation of happiness and misery, and the reductio that a merciful principle consistently applied would have to reach the devil himself.
passages.notes: The chapter heading is at artifact line 17748. Augustine's report of what 'the Church' condemned in Origen is his own summary and is not a citation of a conciliar act; the nearest conciliar-style text registered elsewhere in this library is the 543 Constantinopolitan canon printed by Denzinger at DS 411.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17958-18013: why no cleansing was tolerated for the devil, the appeal to Matthew 25:41 and Apocalypse 20:10, the statement that 'everlasting' and 'for ever' in Scripture mean nothing else than endless duration, the argument that a sentence pronounced on men and angels alike cannot be true of the angels and false of the men, and the correlativity argument from Matthew 25:46.
passages.notes: The chapter heading is at artifact lines 17958-17959. This is the locus of the correlativity argument from Matthew 25:46 that later Latin theology repeats. Augustine's supporting appeal in chapter 9 to the threefold Marcan repetition rests on Mark 9:44 and 9:46 in the received text, verses the modern critical text treats as assimilation to 9:48.
